questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the most common realistic outcome of a substantive architecture review?
options: A simple, unconditional approval with nothing further required
An outright rejection of the entire design
Approval with at least one condition attached, even when the overall direction is accepted
No outcome at all — reviews are described as rarely reaching a decision
questions.explain: The lesson states that most substantive designs get at least one condition attached, making "approved with conditions" the most common realistic outcome, not a clean unconditional yes.

questions.q: What does "approved with conditions" actually obligate the presenter to do, per this lesson?
options: Address the specific named items before or during build, while the overall direction proceeds
Scrap the design entirely and start over
Nothing — conditions are treated as optional suggestions with no real obligation
Wait indefinitely for a second review before taking any action
questions.explain: Conditions are specific, named items (like a documented rollback path) that must be addressed before or during build — the direction is accepted, but those items are not optional.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against treating every comment made during a review as an equally binding change request?
options: Because review boards are never allowed to make the same comment twice
Because only written comments submitted after the meeting count as real feedback
Because treating comments as binding is required by the ADR format
Because some comments are questions already answered in the room, and treating all comments as binding can drift the design away from its original intent based on a misunderstanding
questions.explain: Not all review comments are new information — some restate a point already addressed. Treating every comment as equally binding risks revising the design around a misunderstanding rather than a real gap.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say you should return to the original problem statement before revising the design after feedback?
options: Because feedback is only valid relative to the problem the design was actually solving, so checking against it prevents chasing a comment that addresses a different problem
Because the problem statement must be rewritten after every review regardless of feedback
Because the problem statement determines the rollout plan's rollback switch
Because review boards require the problem statement to be presented twice
questions.explain: Feedback is only meaningful relative to the stated problem; a comment that would solve a different problem than the one being addressed isn't a valid reason to change the design's direction.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend a "delta" presentation rather than a full rebuild of the deck when re-presenting a revised design?
options: Because a full rebuild is required by most review boards as a formality

Because showing only what changed in response to specific feedback keeps the conversation focused on confirming that feedback was addressed, without burying it in a full repeat of problem, options, and design
Because delta presentations are shorter and therefore always preferred regardless of content
Because the original deck must never be shown again after the first review
questions.explain: A delta presentation opens with what was asked for and what changed in response, giving the board a short, focused way to confirm their feedback was addressed instead of re-deriving the whole design from scratch.
